What Is Creditor Harassment?

Creditor harassment refers to aggressive or unlawful actions by debt collectors aimed at pressuring individuals to repay debts. These tactics can include incessant phone calls, threats, misleading statements, or contacting third parties about your debt.

Under the Fair Debt Collection Practices Act (FDCPA), creditors are prohibited from engaging in abusive, unfair, or deceptive practices. For example, they cannot call outside of permitted hours, typically between 8 AM and 9 PM, or use profane language during communications.

To stop creditor harassment and other violations of these protections, consider taking legal action. Henkels & Baker PC offers relief to individuals facing relentless harassment.

Understanding Creditor Harassment

Creditor harassment is a significant issue that many debtors face. A Consumer Financial Protection Bureau study revealed that twenty-seven percent of consumers who were approached about debt reported feeling threatened by the actions of the creditor or collector who last contacted them. It can manifest as frequent calls, aggressive communication, and threats from debt collectors. Sometimes, debt collectors employ aggressive tactics to scare individuals into paying. They may threaten lawsuits, disclose your debt to third parties, or use abusive language.

Federal law sets clear boundaries for what debt collectors can do. The Fair Debt Collection Practices Act (FDCPA) forbids harassment and protects your rights. This law includes acceptable debt collector contacts, collection practices, and communication guidelines.

If contacted by a debt collector, verify the debt. Ask for written validation of particular debt and dispute inaccuracies. This step ensures you are not paying for debts you do not owe.

At Henkels & Baker, PC, we have extensive experience dealing with creditor harassment cases. We recognize the emotional and financial strain caused by ongoing harassment from a credit reporting company, and we are here to guide you through this challenging experience.

Your Legal Rights Under the FDCPA

The Fair Debt Collection Practices Act (FDCPA) safeguards individuals facing debt or collection calls. This law ensures debt collection agencies cannot engage in abusive, deceptive, or unfair practices. Knowing your rights can help you navigate stressful interactions with debt collectors and take appropriate action when necessary.

Under the FDCPA, debt collectors are forbidden from:

  • Using threats of violence or harm
  • Disclosing the names of debtors who refuse to settle their debts.
  • Using obscene or profane language
  • Repeatedly calling to annoy or harass

You have the right to dispute the debt in writing. You must notify the collector, but they must only contact you once they verify the debt. Additionally, collectors must provide a detailed validation notice within five days of their initial communication.

If a collection agency has breached the Fair Debt Collection Practices Act (FDCPA), consider filing a complaint to the Federal Trade Commission (FTC) or your state attorney general. In cases of severe violations, legal action is an option. You may sue for damages, including legal fees, in both state and federal courts.

The Consumer Financial Protection Bureau (CFPB) also provides resources and can take action against collectors. If you win a lawsuit, you could be awarded up to $1,000 in statutory damages plus any actual damages you can prove.

Understanding your legal rights under the FDCPA empowers you to protect yourself against unethical debt collection practices.

Steps to Take When Harassed by Creditors

When dealing with unwanted and aggressive contact from creditors, it’s crucial to understand the proactive steps you can take to safeguard yourself and effectively navigate the situation.

  • Document Incidents: When creditor harassment begins, our first step should be documenting every incident. Keep a record of every call, letter, or text. Record the date, time, and other details of each communication. This information can be crucial when disputing the debt or taking legal action.
  • Dispute the Debt: Next, we should dispute the debt if we believe it is invalid. Please submit a written dispute letter to the creditor within 30 days of their initial contact. This letter should request verification of the credit card debt amount, ensuring that the creditor provides proof that the debt is ours.
  • Cease-and-Desist Letter: If harassment continues, we can send a cease-and-desist letter to the debt collector. This letter clearly states that we wish to avoid being contacted further. According to FDCPA, the debt collector must only contact us if they inform us of specific actions, like a lawsuit.
  • Maintain Effective Communication: Effective communication is essential. We should remain calm and professional when we speak or write to creditors. Avoid giving personal, personal, or financial information that could be used against us. Instead, use clear and concise language to express our concerns or requests.
  • Consult an Attorney: If harassment involves threats or lies, it’s time to consult an attorney. The FDCPA protects us from abusive practices; an attorney can help enforce these rights. They can guide us in filing a complaint with the Federal Trade Commission (FTC) or taking legal action against the creditor.

Following these steps can address creditor harassment more effectively and protect our rights.

Legal Remedies to Stop Creditor Harassment

Many individuals face relentless calls and letters from debt collectors. The CFPB debt collection survey reveals that a creditor or debt collector contacted nearly one-third of consumers—over 70 million Americans—regarding a debt in the past year. Additionally, more than one in four consumers reported experiencing threatening communication. Fortunately, there are robust legal remedies available.

Your Rights Under the Fair Debt Collection Practices Act (FDCPA)

Under the Fair Debt Collection Practices Act (FDCPA), you can request that a debt collector stop all personal calls and communications. This can be realized by sending a cease and desist letter. Once this letter is sent, the debt collector must cease phone calls and written correspondence.

Filing a Complaint with the Consumer Financial Protection Bureau (CFPB)

If harassment persists, you may also consider filing a complaint with the Consumer Financial Protection Bureau (CFPB) as an alternative course of action. The CFPB enforces federal laws against abusive financial practices and helps rectify issues through investigation.

Taking Legal Action Against Debt Collectors

Taking legal action to stop debt collectors is also a powerful remedy. Suing debt collectors for harassment under the FDCPA allows you to potentially recover damages and attorney fees. This action holds them accountable and deters future misconduct.

Hiring an attorney ensures you leverage all possible legal avenues. A skilled attorney can guide you through filing a lawsuit, negotiating settlements, and protecting your rights effectively.

Role of Bankruptcy in Stopping Creditor Harassment

Bankruptcy provides a crucial barrier against persistent creditor harassment. A key protective measure is the automatic stay in bankruptcy, which instantly stops all collection efforts, including wage garnishment, foreclosure, and repossession, as outlined in 11 U.S.C. § 362. Debt collectors must cease their efforts once bankruptcy is filed, providing instant relief to those overwhelmed by unpaid debt.

Chapter 7 Bankruptcy

Chapter 7 bankruptcy, often called liquidation bankruptcy, allows people to discharge most of their debts and start anew. This is clearly outlined in 11 U.S.C. § 727, which specifies the conditions for granting a debtor’s discharge. The statute states that a discharge relieves a debtor from personal liability for most debts, freeing them from the legal obligation to repay.

This type can wipe out unsecured debts like credit card balances and medical bills, stopping creditors from pursuing collection efforts on old debts. However, certain obligations, such as student loans, child support, and taxes, generally cannot be discharged in bankruptcy.

Chapter 13 Bankruptcy

Chapter 13, known as reorganization bankruptcy, involves creating a repayment plan to repay debts over time, typically three to five years. Under 11 U.S.C. § 1322(d)(1), the repayment plan must typically extend for five years if a debtor’s current monthly income exceeds the applicable state median.

More so, a plan can only allow for payments over five years. The law bars creditors from initiating or continuing collection activities throughout this period. This plan helps collect debt, protect assets from liquidation, and allow for rescheduling secured debts, such as mortgages. It ensures that creditors receive structured payments, reducing the harassment associated with debt collection.

Engaging a bankruptcy attorney can streamline the process, ensuring appropriate filings and maximizing available protections. Professional legal assistance is essential for navigating the complexities of bankruptcy law.

Choosing the Right Legal Representation

Selecting the right attorney for creditor harassment cases is crucial. Finding someone with experience in debt collection laws and a verifiable record of success in similar cases is essential. This ensures that your rights will be defended robustly and efficiently.

When facing debt collector harassment, we recommend seeking a lawyer practicing this field. They should know the Fair Debt Collection Practices Act (FDCPA) and other relevant regulations. An experienced attorney can help navigate the complexities of the law and guide you through the legal action required.

Here are some essential considerations:  

  • Experience: Choose a lawyer with a proven history of handling creditor harassment cases.
  • Reputation: Look for positive client testimonials and feedback.
  • Specialization: Ensure the attorney practices creditor harassment and debt relief.

Sometimes, taking legal action might involve filing a lawsuit against a debt collection business or agency for violations. It’s vital to have legal representation that understands the nuances of these lawsuits. Misrepresentation by debt collectors can be a basis for your case, and a knowledgeable attorney will know how to leverage this.
